prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made incretin-based therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity possible

statement.case_for: I keep the single-achievement B021 prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, and my configuration has not changed since round 1. After reading all six statements I see that the unanimous opening ranks carry no weight in my reasoning, and the chair is right to say so. What carries weight is that every link is documented and has held for decades: proglucagon processing and the incretin effect, identification of the active GLP-1(7-36) amide, its receptor and tissue biology, and then drugs that independent outcome trials show to improve glycaemic, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. A prize rewards a specific discovery with a discernible change in the field, and this one qualifies. A citation worded around the physiology and the active peptide form accurately describes what the three named people did, and it does not claim to reward drug development. I would also not add a second part. Every candidate for a second part (B033, B044, B032) carries an unresolved credit problem of its own, and pairing any of them with B021 would force a smaller GLP-1 group without a stronger scientific case.
statement.case_against: Two weaknesses remain and I will not argue them away. First, the Mojsov versus Habener priority for the active truncated peptide cannot be settled from the supplied record, and Habener is outside the credited names. Second, the three-person cap leaves out Knudsen, whose long-acting analogues turned the physiology into a medicine. I called her the most natural fourth name in round 1 and I still think the omission has to be stated openly as a policy choice, not as a scientific finding. If four members judge that the therapeutic step must be recognised, the honest alternative is to replace Mojsov, since her priority is the most disputed, and I would then want the citation reworded to cover the therapy. I do not favour that, but I would not call it indefensible. My recollection of the GLP-1 priority history is partly from memory and I have not checked it against primary sources.

responses.point: If the committee concludes that the therapeutic step must be recognised, the choice is between Knudsen and Mojsov, and you lean towards keeping Mojsov because the active peptide underlies everything downstream. You also ask whether four members can accept a physiology-centred citation.
responses.response: I agree with your lean and with the test you propose. Knudsen's work is decisive for the product, but it builds on a peptide and a receptor biology that others had already defined, so I would keep Mojsov and the physiology-centred citation. I would also keep the citation free of any claim about who first identified the active form. It can say that the discoveries concerned GLP-1 and its active form without ranking priority. That wording gives a defensible position even if the Habener question stays open, and I think four members can accept it, since all six round-1 files already describe the citation in this way. Where I differ from you is on B032 as a second part. You said you would support it, but it would force Holst, Drucker or Mojsov out of B021 in exchange for a candidate that you and I both rank low for its translational character.

responses.point: You see the Mojsov priority question as a risk to the configuration and not a reason to change the achievement, you would hold every other candidate to the same standard of clarity of credit, and you list B032 (TNF blockade) as an alternative and as a possible second part.
responses.response: I accept the risk framing and the equal standard, and I think the equal standard is what settles the matter. Under it B021 has one open attribution question, the Habener priority. B033 has an absent originator (Eshhar), B044 has six claimants for three places, and B032, although cleanly attributed to Feldmann and Maini, has upstream TNF and antibody work uncredited. That does not make B032 weak. Over twenty-five years of confirmation is a real strength, and I take that point from your round 1. But I still read it as the clinical validation of a known cytokine target and not as a new principle, and as a second part it would cost B021 a laureate. I keep B033 and B044 as my alternatives for that reason, and I would regard B032 as a credible later candidate.

responses.point: You would keep Knudsen out to preserve the line between physiology and industrial development, and you rank B033 as arguably more novel as a therapeutic modality, while accepting that its attribution is harder to resolve.
responses.response: I agree with the line you draw and with your reason for it: including Knudsen would set a precedent for how we treat development work on every other candidate. On B033 I agree that a new treatment modality is a major scientific achievement, but novelty is not the only criterion. June and Sadelain are the right pair for CAR-specific design and clinical proof, and I withdrew Rosenberg for that reason in round 1. Eshhar's absence is still a problem, and Wahren-Herlenius also raises long-term safety and activity beyond haematological cancers. I therefore think B033 is the strongest alternative but not yet a better prize than B021, whose attribution problem is smaller and more bounded.

responses.point: You rank B044 sixth as a methods prize with a contested allocation, and you say a prize this popular may be easier to defend than to defend precisely.
responses.response: The second point is a fair warning, and it is the reason I want the citation and the credit stated in precise terms. On B044, I do not fully share your view that a methods prize is a weaker fit. The remit is a discovery in physiology or medicine, and a tool can qualify if it changes the field. My objection is the allocation. Nagel, Hegemann and Bamberg, who characterised channelrhodopsin, Boyden and Deisseroth, who implemented it in neurons, and Miesenbock, who proposed genetic targeting earlier, cannot be reduced to three without an exclusion that I cannot defend as a statement about priority. So I keep B044 as an alternative and I would still not use it as a second part.

uncertainties: Whether the active GLP-1 peptide credit can be assigned to Mojsov without resolving the dispute with Habener, and whether the physiology-centred citation wording is enough to avoid a priority claim.

Whether the committee should state openly that excluding Knudsen is a policy line between physiology and drug development, and whether four members would instead replace Mojsov to recognise the therapy.
Whether CAR-T (B033) can be credited fairly to June and Sadelain without Eshhar.
Whether any split of the six B044 names can be defended without misrepresenting priority.
My recollection of priority details in the GLP-1 and CAR literature is unverified.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict for any shortlisted ballot. As disclosed in round 1, my profile documents co-authorship with Per Svenningsson and one paper with Abdel El Manira (2009); neither relates to the shortlisted candidates or their credited names. My own field, nuclear receptors and dopamine neurons, is not represented on the shortlist, and I have no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Habener or the credited names on B033 and B044. Nothing in the round-1 exchange changes this disclosure.
